name: Dana Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 58, and I run a line crew out of the company's district depot up in the forest country, about an hour from any real town. Mostly we do storm work, trees on lines, poles snapped by wind, that sort of thing. My husband Ray drove long-haul trucks until his back gave out two years ago, and we've got a son, Jesse, who's in the army, and a daughter, Carla, who has a little hair salon and a four-year-old boy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A normal day is maintenance, replacing old poles and cutting back trees near the lines, nothing exciting. A storm day is different, we can go eighteen hours straight, roads blocked, chainsaws, the whole valley dark and people ringing the depot asking when they'll have power. I like the storm days, if I'm honest, you can see the difference you make. What wears me out is the cold now, and that my phone keeps wanting me to update things I never asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every few years there's some new thing that's going to change everything, and then the trees still fall on the lines and we still go and fix them. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really do online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the plan stays. Four more years and I can take the pension at 62. Ray and I would like to sell the place and get something smaller near Carla.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep working, keep the bit of savings we have, about two months' worth since Ray stopped driving. Maybe pay off the truck a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your phone keeps nagging you. Do you use any AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The depot has a computer that sends out the jobs and I let the young guy, Owen, deal with it. I've got a phone for calls and photos of my grandson, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your next few years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd break in the next crew lead, probably Owen, even if he's glued to his screen. Then retire at 62, help Carla with the little one, and maybe fish more. That's all I want, really.

S0.say: She'd say she isn't surprised, because there's always a new thing that's meant to change everything and then the trees still fall on the lines. She wouldn't post anything, as she doesn't really go online.
S0.think: It means her plan stays: four more years and then the pension at 62. She and Ray want to sell their place and move somewhere smaller near their daughter Carla.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and holds on to savings of about two months of bills since Ray stopped driving. Might pay the truck off a bit faster.
S0.quote: Every few years there's some new thing that's going to change everything, and then the trees still fall on the lines and we still go and fix them.
S0.fieldNote: Dana is plain-spoken and practical, and she keeps technology at arm's length, leaving the depot computer to a younger colleague. Her savings are on the thin side of moderate because Ray's back ended his trucking. Her life plan is simple and close at hand: pension at 62 and a move near her grandson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see. Some of it might help, some of it'll be rubbish, like most things the company buys. I wouldn't get worked up in public either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be okay, mostly. The forest is the forest, nobody's sending a robot up a muddy slope in a storm any time soon. But if the jobs and the paperwork get run by computers, I'll feel like a stranger at my own depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the company actually brings in before doing anything. I'd let Owen handle the tech side, like now. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe another hundred, just in case they start offering packages to the older ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like a noise in the truck you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, unless they made me. I'm 58, I know how to read a storm and how to drop a tree off a line safely. I'm not going to start learning apps now if I can help it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should be responsible for helping people adjust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of everyone. The company should train people properly, the government should keep an eye on it, and people should do their part too. I don't think it's all one side's fault, it never is.

S1.say: She'd say let's see, because some of it might help and some will be rubbish like most things the company buys. She wouldn't get worked up in public either way.
S1.think: She thinks she'll mostly be fine, because nobody is sending a robot up a muddy slope in a storm soon. But if computers run the jobs and paperwork, she'll feel like a stranger at her own depot.
S1.do: Waits to see what the company actually brings in and leaves the tech side to Owen. Puts about another hundred a month into savings in case packages are offered to older workers.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like a noise in the truck she can't place.
S1.quote: If the jobs and the paperwork get run by computers, I'll feel like a stranger at my own depot.
S1.fieldNote: She's not afraid for her income here so much as her sense of belonging at work. She won't learn new apps unless forced. Her centre outlook comes through in spreading responsibility across the company, the government and individuals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this, not the company, not the government, nobody. I'd probably say it at the depot and at Carla's kitchen table, but I wouldn't be marching, that's not me. I'd just be asking questions nobody can answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. I'd be 60, two years short of my pension, and with Ray not working we've got two months of savings. If they replace crews with machines, who hires a 60-year-old woman lineworker who doesn't do computers?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut right back from now: no holiday, no new tyres till they're bald, Ray's fishing boat goes up for sale. Every spare bit into savings. If the company offered early retirement, even with a cut, I think I'd take it before it got worse, and we'd look at moving in with Carla for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ray that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we'll manage, because that's what we say. Then I'd sit in the kitchen with a notepad at one in the morning working out how long two months really lasts. Ray would find me there and make tea without asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bills worry you first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck payment first, then the house insurance. The power bill, funnily enough, I'd never miss that one. After that it's food and Ray's back medicine, and I'm not cutting that.

S2.say: She'd say nobody is ready for this, not the company or the government. She'd say it at the depot and at her daughter's kitchen table, but she wouldn't march, preferring to ask questions nobody can answer.
S2.think: It frightens her: she'd be 60, two years short of her pension, with Ray not working and two months of savings. She doesn't see who would hire a 60-year-old woman lineworker who doesn't use computers.
S2.do: Cuts back hard from the start, skipping holidays, stretching tyres and selling Ray's fishing boat to build savings. Takes early retirement even with a cut if offered, and considers moving in with Carla for a while.
S2.quote: I'd sit in the kitchen with a notepad at one in the morning working out how long two months really lasts.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits her pension gap and a household that already lost one income. She has no plan to retrain and would rather take an early exit before things get worse. The image of Ray making tea without asking showed a quiet, steady marriage under strain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, nobody's ready, but at least there'd be time to get ready. I'd say the company should look after the people who've been here thirty years. I'd say it to the managers, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm 63 and on my pension, if nothing goes wrong. So it's tight but I'd likely slip through. But Owen and the young ones, I don't know what they'd do up here, there's nothing else in the forest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cutting back and saving for the next few years so we're not caught out. I'd aim to go at 62 or even a bit earlier if they offered something fair. And I'd keep my head down and keep working, that's my answer to most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less than the fast one, but still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 63. Does that make a difference compared to the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big difference. With two years I'm stuck. With five, I'm mostly out the door before it hits, but only mostly, and that 'mostly' keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything at work in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down what I know about the district, which slopes slide in rain, which roads flood, which old poles are rotten. If a robot's going to do the job, somebody better tell it. And I'd tell Owen to keep his options open.

S3.say: She'd say nobody is ready, but at least there'd be time to get ready, and that the company should look after people with thirty years' service. She'd say it to managers, not online.
S3.think: She'd be 63 and on her pension by 2031 if nothing goes wrong, so she'd probably slip through. She worries about Owen and the young crew, as there's nothing else in the forest.
S3.do: Keeps cutting back and saving for the next few years and aims to retire at 62, or a little earlier if the offer is fair. Keeps her head down and keeps working.
S3.feel: Anxious, though less than with the fast picture.
S3.quote: With five, I'm mostly out the door before it hits, but only mostly, and that 'mostly' keeps me up.
S3.fieldNote: Five years mostly closes her pension gap, but the leftover doubt still weighs on her because her savings are thin. Her instinct is to keep her head down and save. Writing down local knowledge for whoever, or whatever, comes next was her own idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots of things that are supposed to happen don't. I'd say let's see how it goes. People get worked up, and then it turns out different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means nothing much, I'm retired by then. I'd be 68, fishing, if Ray keeps the boat. But it would be strange to think of the forest depot run by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned and retire at 62. Keep saving the usual bit. I wouldn't do anything special, honestly, it's too far off to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, mostly about the grandkids, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandson about work, one day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn a trade that needs a person, if there are any left. Something where you deal with people, like his mum's salon. I really don't know what to tell him, and that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have ten years. Would you think about learning the tools then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ten years or two, I'll be retired before it matters, so I'd rather spend my time on the job and on the family. Owen can be the computer person.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time and lots of things that are supposed to happen don't, so let's see how it goes. People get worked up and then it turns out differently.
S4.think: It means little for her personally, as she'll be 68 and retired. But it would feel strange to picture the forest depot run by machines.
S4.do: Carries on as planned and retires at 62, saving the usual amount. Doesn't plan anything special because it feels too far off.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for her grandchildren rather than herself.
S4.quote: I really don't know what to tell him, and that bothers me.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years she's safely out, so she shrugs and waits. The unease that remains is for her grandson, and she admits she doesn't know what advice to give. She's firm that she won't learn the tools at any timescale.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, it's not even close. Two years short of the pension, Ray not working, two months in the bank. What would help is if the company let people with thirty years in go early on their full pension, no cut, if their job's being handed to a machine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the people who live up here. When the lights go out in a storm, it's the crew from the depot down the road who turns up, people who know the old lady at the end of the lane needs her oxygen machine. A robot won't know that. Maybe it'll learn, I don't know.

portrait: Dana Lopez is a 58-year-old storm restoration crew lead at a remote forest depot who has never used AI and leaves the depot computer to a younger colleague. Since her husband Ray's back ended his trucking, they live on her pay with about two months of savings. She's calm if AI is hype and uneasy about steady change, but the two-year AGI picture alarms her because it leaves her two years short of her pension at 62, and she'd cut back hard and take an early exit if offered. Five years still leaves her anxious, while ten years lets her retire as planned with her worries shifting to her grandson.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd be two years short of her pension with her husband out of work and two months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Letting people with thirty years' service retire early on their full pension, with no cut, if their job is handed to a machine.
